body:
Health is more than the absence of disease

Health is a state of physical, mental and social well-being. Physical health involves the proper functioning of the body's organs and systems. Mental health includes emotional well-being and the ability to cope with ordinary challenges. Social well-being depends partly on safe surroundings, supportive relationships and access to essential services.

A person may have no diagnosed disease but still experience poor health because of malnutrition, unsafe housing or severe psychological distress. Therefore, being disease-free and being healthy are not identical.

Health also has a community dimension. Clean drinking water, sanitation, waste disposal, adequate nutrition, vaccination and access to healthcare protect individuals. These conditions cannot always be secured by personal effort alone.

What is a disease?

A disease is a disturbance of normal bodily structure or function that produces identifiable changes. These changes may be noticed by the affected person or detected during medical examination.

  • Symptom: A change experienced or reported by a person, such as headache, nausea or fatigue.
  • Sign: A finding that can be observed or measured, such as a rash, fever recorded by a thermometer or elevated blood pressure.
  • Cause: The factor responsible for producing a disease. Causes may include pathogens, nutritional deficiencies, genetic changes and environmental or behavioural factors.
  • Risk factor: A condition that increases the likelihood of disease but does not necessarily cause disease in every exposed person.

For example, a cough is a symptom rather than a specific diagnosis. It can occur with a common viral infection, tuberculosis, asthma or other conditions. The same symptom may therefore arise from different diseases.

Two independent ways of classifying diseases

Diseases are commonly classified by their cause and by their duration. These are separate classifications, not competing alternatives.

BasisCategoryMeaning and example
CauseInfectiousCaused by a pathogen; examples include tuberculosis and malaria.
CauseNon-infectiousNot caused by a pathogen; examples include diabetes and scurvy.
DurationAcuteDevelops or lasts for a relatively short period; the common cold is an example.
DurationChronicPersists or has prolonged effects; examples include asthma, diabetes and some infectious diseases.

An infectious disease may be acute or chronic. Tuberculosis is infectious and can have a prolonged course. Asthma is chronic but is not an infectious disease. Therefore, chronic does not mean noncommunicable.

Infectious and communicable are related but not identical

An infectious disease is caused by an infectious agent. A communicable disease is an infectious disease that can spread from an infected source to another susceptible host, directly or indirectly.

Some infectious diseases are not ordinarily transmitted from one infected person to another. Tetanus, caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, is usually acquired when bacterial spores from the environment enter a wound. It is infectious but is not spread through ordinary person-to-person contact.

Another useful distinction concerns the relationship between an immediate cause and underlying conditions. An intestinal infection may directly cause diarrhoea, while contaminated water, inadequate sanitation and poor nutrition contribute to the likelihood or severity of illness. Effective prevention must therefore address both the pathogen and the conditions that allow disease to occur.

Prelims focus

  • Health includes physical, mental and social well-being.
  • A symptom is experienced or reported; a sign is observed or measured.
  • Infectious versus non-infectious describes causation; acute versus chronic describes duration.
  • Tuberculosis is an example of an infectious disease that may be chronic.
  • Trap: Tetanus is infectious but is not ordinarily communicable from person to person.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, sections 13.1–13.3; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, introduction and section 8.1; WHO, Tetanus, fact sheet dated 15 July 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Health, Disease and the Classification of Illnesses

body:
Pathogens and infection

A pathogen is a biological agent capable of causing disease. Pathogens may enter the body through inhalation, contaminated food or water, injured skin, insect bites or contact involving certain body fluids.

Infection occurs when a pathogen enters and establishes itself in a host. Infection does not always produce noticeable illness. Some infected individuals have mild symptoms or no symptoms, but certain infections can still spread to others.

Different pathogens produce different diseases. Knowing both the organism and the route of transmission is essential because the appropriate prevention method depends on them.

Major groups of human pathogens

Bacteria

Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms. Many are harmless or beneficial, but pathogenic bacteria cause diseases such as tuberculosis, typhoid and cholera. Some bacterial infections can be treated using appropriately selected antibiotics.

Viruses

Viruses require living host cells to reproduce. Viral diseases include measles, influenza, dengue and HIV infection. Antibiotics that act on bacteria do not cure these viral infections.

Protozoa

Protozoa are generally single-celled eukaryotic organisms. The malaria parasite belongs to the genus Plasmodium. Entamoeba histolytica can cause amoebiasis.

Fungi

Some fungi cause infections of the skin, hair or nails. Ringworm is a familiar example. Despite its name, ringworm is caused by fungi known as dermatophytes, not by worms.

Helminths

Helminths are parasitic worms. Roundworms such as Ascaris can cause intestinal infection, while filarial worms such as Wuchereria can cause lymphatic filariasis.

Important disease-organism-transmission relationships

DiseaseCausative agentMain transmission route
TuberculosisMycobacterium tuberculosis; bacteriumAirborne particles from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB
TyphoidSalmonella Typhi; bacteriumFood or water contaminated with human faecal matter
CholeraVibrio cholerae; bacteriumContaminated food or water
MeaslesMeasles virusAirborne spread
DengueDengue virusBite of an infected Aedes mosquito
MalariaPlasmodium; protozoan parasiteBite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
AmoebiasisEntamoeba histolytica; protozoan parasiteFaecally contaminated food or water
AscariasisAscaris lumbricoides; roundwormSwallowing infective eggs from contaminated soil, food or water
Lymphatic filariasisFilarial worms, including WuchereriaBites of infected mosquitoes
RingwormDermatophyte fungiContact with infected skin, animals or contaminated objects

Pathogen and vector must not be confused

A vector is a living organism that carries a pathogen between hosts. Mosquitoes are vectors for several human diseases. However, the mosquito is not necessarily the organism that causes the disease.

Malaria is caused by a protozoan parasite, not by a mosquito. The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the parasite during a bite. Dengue is caused by a virus, while Aedes mosquitoes, particularly Aedes aegypti, act as important vectors.

Aedes mosquitoes commonly bite during daylight hours and can breed in small collections of water in containers. This is why removing stagnant water from domestic surroundings is an important preventive measure against dengue.

The severity of an infection depends on the pathogen, the amount and route of exposure, and the host's immunity and general health. A pathogen's presence does not guarantee that every exposed person will develop the same symptoms.

Prelims focus

  • Typhoid and cholera are bacterial diseases.
  • Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan parasite.
  • Dengue is viral; the important vector is Aedes aegypti.
  • Malaria is transmitted by an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
  • Ringworm is fungal, whereas ascariasis is caused by a parasitic worm.
  • Trap: A mosquito is the vector of malaria, not its causative pathogen.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections 2.1 and 2.4; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.1, Common Diseases in Humans; WHO, Malaria, questions and answers dated 4 December 2025; National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control, Vector of Dengue Fever; WHO, Tuberculosis, fact sheet; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Malaria is caused by a parasite and transmitted by a mosquito vector.

title: Disease-Causing Organisms and Common Communicable Diseases

body:
Why the route of transmission matters

A communicable disease spreads only when its pathogen reaches another susceptible host through a suitable route. Prevention becomes more effective when the route is correctly identified.

For example, providing safe drinking water helps prevent waterborne infections, but it does not replace mosquito control for dengue. Similarly, removing mosquito breeding sites does not directly prevent tuberculosis, which spreads through the air.

Main transmission routes

Respiratory transmission

Infected people may release infectious respiratory particles when breathing, speaking, coughing or sneezing. Some particles remain suspended in the air and can be inhaled by others. Tuberculosis and measles are important examples of airborne transmission. Influenza and other respiratory infections can also spread through respiratory particles, especially during close contact or in poorly ventilated places.

Useful preventive measures include good ventilation, appropriate respiratory hygiene, vaccination where available and reducing exposure to infectious individuals. Particular measures depend on the disease.

Foodborne and waterborne transmission

When human faecal matter contaminates drinking water or food, pathogens can enter the digestive system. This route is often called faecal-oral transmission.

Typhoid, cholera, amoebiasis and ascariasis illustrate infections associated with contaminated food, water or soil. Prevention requires safe water, toilets, proper sewage disposal, handwashing with soap, clean food preparation and safe food storage.

Vector-borne transmission

A vector transmits an infectious agent between hosts. Important mosquito-borne diseases include malaria, dengue, chikungunya and lymphatic filariasis.

  • Malaria: Preventing bites by infected Anopheles mosquitoes is essential. Insecticide-treated mosquito nets are an important preventive measure where appropriate.
  • Dengue: Reducing breeding sites of Aedes mosquitoes, protecting against daytime mosquito bites and covering water containers are important.

Discarded tyres, flowerpot trays, uncovered water containers and coolers may collect water suitable for mosquito breeding. Removing or managing such water addresses transmission at the community level.

Contact and body-fluid transmission

Some infections spread through direct skin contact or contaminated objects, as may occur with ringworm. Others spread through blood or sexual contact. HIV can be transmitted through infected blood and certain sexual fluids, as well as from a mother to her child during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.

Using sterile needles and safe blood supplies, practising safer sex, and providing appropriate antenatal services reduce these risks.

Breaking the chain of infection

The spread of infection can be understood through 3 connected requirements: an infectious source, a route of transmission and a susceptible host. Interrupting any necessary link can reduce transmission.

  • Source control: Early identification of infectious cases and appropriate public-health measures reduce the opportunity for spread.
  • Route control: Safe water, sanitation, ventilation, condoms and vector control interrupt different transmission pathways.
  • Protection of the host: Vaccination, adequate nutrition and other preventive practices reduce susceptibility or the likelihood of severe disease.

No single preventive measure works equally well against all infections. The correct measure depends on the pathogen and how it spreads.

Personal hygiene and public sanitation

Personal hygiene includes handwashing, hygienic food handling and keeping the body clean. Public sanitation includes sewage treatment, solid-waste management, safe community water supplies and drainage.

Both are necessary. A household may practise good handwashing, yet remain exposed to infection if its only water source is contaminated. Conversely, a safe community water supply cannot fully compensate for unsafe food handling within the household.

Prelims focus

  • Faecal-oral transmission is associated with contaminated food or water.
  • Tuberculosis is primarily an airborne infection.
  • Vector control is particularly relevant to malaria and dengue.
  • Aedes mosquitoes commonly bite during daylight hours.
  • Sanitation is a public-health intervention, not merely an individual hygiene practice.
  • Trap: Mosquito control cannot replace safe drinking water for preventing cholera.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, section 13.3, Infectious Diseases; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.1; National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control, Vector of Dengue Fever and dengue prevention information; WHO, Tuberculosis, fact sheet; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Prevention can interrupt infection at the source, route or susceptible host.

title: Routes of Disease Transmission and Principles of Prevention

body:
The body's defence against infection

Humans are continuously exposed to microorganisms, but every exposure does not produce disease. The body has several protective mechanisms, collectively described as immunity.

The immune system recognises and responds to harmful agents. It includes physical barriers, specialised cells and molecules that help prevent infection or limit its effects.

Innate immunity and acquired immunity

FeatureInnate immunityAcquired immunity
PresencePresent from birthDevelops after antigen exposure or is acquired through transfer of ready-made antibodies
SpecificityBroad, relatively non-specific defenceSpecific response to particular antigens
ExamplesSkin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytic cellsAntibodies and antigen-specific immune cells
MemoryNo antigen-specific memory of the usual adaptive kindCan produce immune memory and a stronger later response

Antigens are substances or structures recognised by the immune system. Antibodies are proteins produced by B lymphocytes that bind specifically to particular antigens. T lymphocytes perform other important functions, including helping coordinate immune responses and acting against infected cells.

Active and passive immunity

Active immunity develops when a person's own immune system responds to an infection or a vaccine. It can produce memory cells that respond more rapidly during later exposure. The strength and duration of protection vary between infections and vaccines.

Passive immunity results when protective antibodies are received from another source. Examples include maternal antibodies transferred to a baby and certain antibody preparations used for medical protection. Passive protection is usually immediate but temporary because the recipient has not generated the same immune memory through that antibody transfer.

How vaccination works

A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or component of a pathogen, or to instructions that allow an antigen to be produced. This stimulates an immune response without requiring the person to experience the disease the vaccine is intended to prevent.

Vaccines may prevent infection, reduce the probability of illness or protect especially against severe disease. Protection varies by vaccine, disease and individual.

Examples of vaccine-preventable diseases include measles, polio, diphtheria, tetanus and hepatitis B. The BCG vaccine is important particularly for protecting young children against severe forms of tuberculosis. It does not guarantee complete protection against all forms of TB.

Vaccines and antibiotics serve different purposes

Vaccination is primarily a preventive intervention. Antibiotics are medicines used against susceptible bacterial infections. They do not treat viral infections such as influenza or dengue.

Unnecessary antibiotic use and incorrect use can promote antimicrobial resistance, which means microorganisms become less responsive to medicines previously effective against them. Antibiotics should therefore be used according to appropriate medical advice.

A vaccine trains the immune response before possible disease exposure. An antibiotic acts against a susceptible bacterial infection. These are different mechanisms and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Individual and community protection

Vaccination directly protects vaccinated people and, for some transmissible infections, can also reduce circulation of the pathogen in a population. This indirect protection is often called community immunity. Its extent depends on vaccine performance, coverage and the way the infection spreads.

Maintaining high vaccination coverage is therefore a public-health responsibility as well as an individual preventive measure.

Prelims focus

  • Innate immunity provides broad protection from birth.
  • Acquired immunity can be antigen-specific and produce immune memory.
  • Active immunity involves the person's own immune response; passive immunity involves transferred antibodies.
  • BCG mainly protects young children against severe forms of tuberculosis.
  • Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria, not viruses.
  • Trap: Vaccination does not guarantee that every vaccinated person will never become infected.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, sections 8.2.1–8.2.6, Immunity and Vaccination; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections on medicinal uses of microorganisms and vaccines; WHO, Tuberculosis, fact sheet; sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Active immunity takes time and may form immune memory; transferred antibodies give immediate passive protection that fades as they disappear.
pictures.caption: Active immunity develops through the body's response; passive immunity transfers existing antibodies.
